vignette:
The patient is a 63-year-old African man, a retired journalist, who comes to therapy at his wife’s urging. He sits stiffly on the edge of the chair, hands clasped, eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. He speaks carefully, as if each word costs him something. After several sessions, he begins to tell his story.

He was a senior correspondent for a major news agency, covering conflict and political unrest across the continent. Eighteen months ago, he and his 34-year-old son—a promising freelance photojournalist—were embedded together during a protest in a West African capital. They had done this many times before, father and son, sharing tips on staying safe. On that day, a car bomb detonated near a government building. The blast threw him against a wall. He remembers the ringing silence, the taste of dust, the sight of his son’s camera lying a few feet away, its lens shattered. He does not remember finding the body. He was told later that his son died instantly.

Since then, he has not written a single story. He has not opened his laptop. He avoids the television—the news, especially, but also dramas and documentaries, because anything with a loud noise or a crowd makes his heart race. He cannot listen to the radio. His wife tries to talk about their son, but he cuts her off or walks out of the room. He feels a cold wall rise between them. He knows she is grieving too, but he cannot be there for her. He is ashamed of this.

He has nightmares nearly every night. In the dream, he is standing at the edge of the crowd, and his son is waving him forward. He always wants to shout, “Stop! Don’t go!” but no sound comes out. Then the blast. He wakes drenched in sweat, fists clenched. Sometimes he stays awake the rest of the night, staring at the ceiling, listening to the quiet of the house.

During the day, he feels a constant churning inside—a knot in his stomach, a tightness across his chest. He startles when a car backfires outside, or when his wife’s phone rings unexpectedly. He has stopped going to the market or to mosque. He cannot tolerate being in a room with more than a few people. He once snapped at a neighbor who asked about his son. He avoids any mention of journalism, photography, or West Africa. A calendar in his study still shows that year; he cannot bring himself to turn the page.

He tells the therapist that he used to be a man who chased the truth, who believed stories mattered. Now he cannot bear to read the headlines. He feels hollowed out, like a building after a fire—only the shell remains. He blames himself: It was his idea to get closer to the rally. “I should have known,” he says, his voice breaking for the first time. “I was the experienced one. I should have protected him.”

His wife says he is not the same man she married. He agrees. Sometimes he thinks he is no longer anyone at all. He came to therapy because she asked, but he does not expect it to help. He sits in the chair, his hands still clasped, waiting for the hour to be over.
